job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Gareth Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my grandfather above the family restaurant, the Golden Ladle, in Wexcombe. I'm up at six to help with deliveries, then I do the restaurant's books at the little desk in the back before the lunch rush. After the rush I sit down and do applications, usually until my mother tells me to eat. I don't go out much, because working is how I was raised.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what do you want?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Accounting, and I finished top of my class. I did one internship in the accounts team at a regional builders' merchant, and one at a small firm of accountants, Fenner and Lowe, doing year-end files. I want a proper job with a firm that has been around a while, where I can learn the trade from older people and stay for years. My father says I should join the restaurant, but I want to earn my own wage first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, which we call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I thought. Computers have been 'about to change everything' for thirty years. I'd tell people to keep working and not chase every new gadget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm still anxious, because my problem is not AI, it's that nobody has hired me. I've been applying for seven months. I have some debt and about two months saved, and my father would help, but I don't like taking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am: apply to local firms, walk in with my CV where I can, and phone to follow up. I'd go back to Fenner and Lowe and ask whether they have a busy-season place. And I'd keep the restaurant's accounts tidy, since that's my practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, mostly in the evenings. I try not to take it out on my family, and I try to look busy. I feel I should have a job by now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do if no firm takes you on by spring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd work at the restaurant full-time for a while. It's honest work and the family needs the help. But I did four years of accounting, and I'd feel like I'd given up if I stayed in the restaurant for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about the restaurant as a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. I love my father, and I respect what he built, but he works seventy hours a week and has a bad back. I don't want that for me. If I take it over, I'd want it to be my choice and not because nothing else came up.

say: I'd say computers have been about to change everything for **thirty years**, so keep working.
I'd tell people not to chase every new **gadget**.
think: My problem isn't AI, it's that **nobody has hired me**.
I don't like taking my **father's help**, even though he'd give it.
do: Apply to local firms and **walk in** with my CV where possible.
Ask **Fenner and Lowe** about busy-season work.
Keep the restaurant's **accounts** tidy as practice.
feel: **Tight in the chest**, mostly in the evenings, feeling I should have a job by now.
S0.quote: I did four years of accounting, and I'd feel like I'd given up if I stayed in the restaurant for good.
fieldNote: Gareth's worry is **pride and timing**, not technology; he says he should have a job by now.
The restaurant is both a safety net and a source of quiet shame.
He treats new tech with dry scepticism, consistent with his resistant stance.

steps.text: Walk into local accounting firms with my CV
Ask Fenner and Lowe for a busy-season place
Keep doing the restaurant's accounts and apply in the afternoons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of fuss, but I know it's real. Firms will use programs for the routine accounts, and they'll still need someone to sign. I'd tell people to respect experience and not push older staff out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm uneasy in a way I'd not say aloud. The jobs I'm applying for are the ones that software could take. I'm not good with new gadgets, and I know it, and I don't like the idea that I'd have to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending to the bone, and put what I earn from the odd bookkeeping job into savings. I'd ask for a place at a small, steady firm where they train people and don't chase the newest thing. And I'd learn the one program the firm uses, slowly, because if I have to, I'll do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed in a quiet way. It's like being told the road is changing while I'm halfway across. I'd rather be told plainly what's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a firm like Fenner and Lowe do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd keep the juniors and train them on both the old and new ways, so there's someone who knows what the program is doing. Fenner and Lowe has two partners and six staff, and they trust people they know. If I'd been there a year, I think they'd keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about learning the new software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it, but I'd do it. I learned the old accounting package from my uncle, and I can learn another. My problem is that I don't trust a program I can't see inside. If it makes a mistake, who explains it to the tax office?

say: I'd say it's a lot of fuss, but it's real, and firms should not push **older staff** out.
I'd say someone still has to **sign** the accounts.
think: The jobs I'm applying for are the ones that **software** could take.
I'm not good with new gadgets, and I don't like having to **be**.
do: Cut spending to the bone and put the **bookkeeping money** into savings.
Ask for a place at a small, steady firm that **trains people**.
Learn the one **program** the firm uses, slowly and properly.
feel: **Alarmed** in a quiet way, like the road changing while I'm halfway across.
S1.quote: I don't trust a program I can't see inside.
fieldNote: Gareth hides his unease from family and says so, a gap between **say and think**.
His trust is in people he knows: small firm, two partners, a year of service.
Distrust of black-box programs is a concrete, accountability-based reason for his resistance.

steps.text: Save the bookkeeping income every month
Apply to small steady firms that train juniors
Learn the one program the firm uses, slowly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should not panic, and the government should look after the people who get hit. I'd say people should keep their heads, keep working, and look after family. I'd say it, but I wouldn't believe my own voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. Everything I trained for is thinking work, and that's what it takes in two years. I'd wonder what a person like me is for, if a machine does the books better. My father's restaurant would last longer, but even he buys from suppliers who use software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything extra and move my savings somewhere safe, then ask my father for full-time hours at the Golden Ladle to keep us going. I'd keep applying, but I'd also start learning from my father how to run the restaurant properly, so I'm useful. And I'd keep the family together, because that's what counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and sort of stunned. It's like being told the factory is closing the day after you got your qualification. I'd feel I'd been sent in the wrong direction by everyone who told me to study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your parents the night you hear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit them down at the table after the dinner shift and say it plainly. My grandfather would say they've lived through bad times before, and my mother would start cooking more. I'd say I'm going to work and we'll manage, and I'd mean it, even if I wasn't sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first thing you stop doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out, new clothes, and the little I pay on the gym. Then I'd stop saving into the pension scheme, if I had started it. I'd keep the phone and the train pass, because I need those to look for work.

say: I'd say people should keep their heads, keep working and **look after family**.
I'd say the government should look after the people who get **hit**.
think: I'm **scared**, because everything I trained for is thinking work.
I'd wonder what a person like me is **for**, if a machine does the books better.
do: Stop extras and move savings to a **safe account**.
Ask my father for **full-time hours** at the Golden Ladle.
Learn from my father how to **run the restaurant** properly.
feel: **Alarmed** and stunned, like a factory closing the day after I qualified.
S2.quote: I'd feel I'd been sent in the wrong direction by everyone who told me to study.
fieldNote: Gareth's composure is **performed**: he says keep calm but admits he wouldn't believe his own voice.
The family restaurant becomes an anchor, with his father's craft as something he can learn.
Anger is aimed at advice-givers who sent him to study, not at his parents.

steps.text: Stop going out and buying clothes
Move savings into a safe account
Work full-time hours at the Golden Ladle and learn the business from my father
Keep sending applications to local firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to train a person if firms start now. I'd say employers should take on apprentices, and I'd tell young people to learn a skill that needs hands. I'd also say schools should teach trades as well as degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious but I could breathe. I could get a job, learn properly and maybe move toward work that has people in it, like advising small businesses. But I know my type of job, the accounts clerk, is a likely casualty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first proper job offered and stay for the full five years. I'd learn the work from the older staff, the things a program can't know. And I'd save a lot, because I want a cushion and I'd like to take over some of the restaurant's business side without being stuck there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed again, but more slowly. It's a long walk toward a cliff, and I'd have time to look for the path. I don't like that you can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do properly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn a job properly: not just entering numbers, but why the numbers matter, and who to call when they don't add up. In five years I'd be a person who knows the clients, and that's worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say a man works, and he doesn't need a degree to know that. But he'd also be proud of me, quietly. He'd say he'd rather see me running the place than sitting in an office that closes.

I'd say employers should take on **apprentices** and schools should teach trades.
think: I'm anxious but I could **breathe**, with time to learn and maybe advise small businesses.
The accounts clerk job is a likely **casualty**.
do: Take the first **proper job** offered and stay the full five years.
Learn from **older staff** what a program can't know.
Save a lot and take on the restaurant's **business side**.
feel: **Alarmed**, but slowly, like a long walk toward a cliff with time to find the path.
S3.quote: In five years I'd be a person who knows the clients, and that's worth something.
fieldNote: Gareth's fix is **apprenticeship**: stay put and learn what a program can't know.
The cliff image shows dread that is slower but unrelieved.
His father's reply is a mix of tradition and pride, which fits the household.

steps.text: Accept the first proper accounting job and stay
Learn client work from the older staff
Save a large part of my pay
Take over the restaurant's business side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time to prepare, and that families and communities should plan together. I'd say churches, clubs and councils should help people who can't. I'd tell young people to get a trade of some kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be calmer than in the others, though not at ease. I'd have a real career and maybe a family. But I'd still wonder whether the office jobs will be gone by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job at a steady firm, qualify as a chartered accountant, and pay down my debt. By year five I'd start learning the software properly, once it has settled. I'd also save for a deposit and perhaps marry, which I can't plan for under the faster ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better. It's the one where I can picture a wedding and a house. It's still uncertain, but at least it isn't a fire alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A career, a family, a bit of land or a flat. I'd like to marry in my late twenties, and I couldn't plan that if I thought the job would vanish in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the warning make you trust the future more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not entirely. Forecasts keep changing, and the people who make them have things to sell. But I'd treat it seriously, the way you treat a weather warning.

I'd say churches, clubs and councils should help those who **can't**.

steps.text: Get a job at a steady firm and qualify as a chartered accountant

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to do things the proper way. A person needs years to learn a trade, and two years is nothing. What would help is simple: firms that keep training young people, jobs that go to those who turn up and work hard, and no sudden surprises.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm tired of being told to adapt like it's a skill you pick up in a weekend. I know how to work. I'd like somebody to give me a job where I can show it.

headlineQuote: I know how to work. I'd like somebody to give me a job where I can show it.
portrait: **Gareth** is a 23-year-old accounting graduate, top of his class, living above his parents' restaurant with his grandfather.
He is **traditional and free-market**, values hard work and apprenticeships, and never uses AI tools.
He does the restaurant's **books** and wants a proper, lasting job at an established firm.
He prefers the familiar, so he **keeps going** and leans on family, not on handouts or new tools.
His mood is anxious now and alarmed when change is fast or near, easing slightly with ten years.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**, because there is no time to learn a trade the proper way.
whatWouldHelp: Firms that **keep training** young people and give jobs to those who turn up and work hard.
**No sudden surprises**: a clear, steady path rather than rapid change.
